1151.quote_or_event: “Without my Beloved, I cannot survive even for an instant; without meeting Him, I cannot sleep.”
1151.explanation: Guru Nanak speaks as the soul-bride who cannot live, or even rest, for a moment apart from her Beloved Lord.
1151.tie_back: The Kural's heroine tells her husband to give news of a swift return only to those who will still be alive, because she will not survive the gap; Guru Nanak's bride likewise says she cannot survive even an instant without the Beloved.
1151.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1274, Raag Malaar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1151._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on 'I cannot survive the parting', though Guru Nanak's Beloved is the Lord and the love is spiritual, not a wife's love for a departing husband.

1152.quote_or_event: “Previously in my spiritual tranquility, I had the happiness and bliss of being near Him, but I am now crying with pangs of separation.”
1152.explanation: Bhai Gurdas, the early Sikh scholar and scribe of the Adi Granth, contrasts the bliss the devotee once knew in the Beloved's presence with the weeping of separation now. His Kabitt Savaiye are early exegesis, not scripture.
1152.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says that his look was once pure delight but that dread of parting now fills even their embrace with pain; Bhai Gurdas sets the same before-and-after of nearness turned to grief.
1152.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabitt Savaiye 670, English translation as given in the BaniDB database
1152._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (kabitt 670); good fit on joy turned to pain, but in the Kural the pain comes from fearing a parting not yet happened, and Bhai Gurdas writes of the soul and the Lord, not of married love.

1153.quote_or_event: “Union with Him, and separation from Him, come by His Will. We come to receive what is written in our destiny.”
1153.explanation: In the Japji Guru Nanak teaches that meeting and parting alike come by the divine order (hukam).
1153.tie_back: The Kural's heroine finds it hard to trust any promise because parting comes in time even with a wise lover; the Japji agrees that separation is built into life, though it asks the Sikh to accept it as hukam rather than lose trust.
1153.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib (pauri 29), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1153._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on the inevitability of parting, but the Japji draws acceptance of the divine will from it, while the Kural draws distrust of a lover's word.

1154.quote_or_event: “In separation, He is not separated from us; He is pervading and permeating amongst all.”
1154.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that the divine Beloved never truly leaves, because He pervades everything, even when the soul feels parted from Him.
1154.tie_back: The Kural's heroine asks whether she is at fault for trusting the one who said 'Do not fear' and then left; Gurbani answers that the divine Beloved who reassures the soul never actually departs, so trust in Him is never misplaced.
1154.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 46, Sri Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1154._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match by contrast only: the Kural is about a human husband breaking his reassurance, while Guru Arjan speaks of a Lord who cannot leave.

1155.quote_or_event: “When the Husband goes away, the bride suffers in the pain of separation”
1155.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the image of a bride left behind when her husband travels to a distant land to describe the soul cut off from the Lord.
1155.tie_back: The Kural's heroine begs her confidante to stop her husband leaving, since once he has gone reunion will be hard; Guru Nanak names exactly that suffering of the bride whose husband has gone away.
1155.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 56, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1155._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa; the line continues in the next verse); reasonable but partial fit, since Guru Nanak describes the pain after the husband leaves rather than a plea to prevent the leaving, and the image is spiritual.

1156.quote_or_event: “He Himself unites us in His Union; there is no more separation.”
1156.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that the Lord Himself brings the soul back into union, and once He does so the separation is over.
1156.tie_back: The Kural's heroine thinks the hope that a husband who can coolly announce his departure will return in kindness is hard to keep; Gurbani holds out the opposite hope, that the divine Beloved Himself ends the separation.
1156.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 37, Sri Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1156._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match by contrast: the Kural doubts the departing lover's grace, while the Guru affirms the Lord's, and it says nothing about a hard-hearted announcement of parting.

1157.quote_or_event: “O black bird, what qualities have made you black? "I have been burnt by separation from my Beloved."”
1157.explanation: Sheikh Farid asks the black koel why it is black, and the bird answers that separation from its Beloved has scorched it, a visible mark of inner longing.
1157.tie_back: In the Kural the bangles slipping from the heroine's wasted wrist proclaim to the town that her husband has left her; in Farid's hymn the bird's blackened body likewise displays the separation it suffers.
1157.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 794, Raag Soohee, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1157._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa; inner quotation marks as in the translation); strong fit on separation written visibly on the body, though Farid's longing is for God and there is no town gossip.

1158.quote_or_event: “Many talk of the pain and suffering of separation; O pain, you are the ruler of all. Fareed, that body, within which love of the Lord does not well up - look upon that body as a cremation ground.”
1158.explanation: Sheikh Farid calls the pain of separation (birha) the sovereign over every other pain, and says a body that never feels it is no better than a cremation ground.
1158.tie_back: The Kural ranks pains, saying living among strangers is bitter but parting from the beloved is bitterer still; Farid likewise crowns the pain of separation as the ruler of all sorrows.
1158.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 36) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1158._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on separation as the greatest pain, but Farid makes no comparison with life among strangers, and his birha is longing for God.

1159.quote_or_event: “The separation of my beloved is not only appearing in my body, like the fire of jungle, but all these dainty dishes and dresses instead of giving me comfort are acting like oil in raising the intensity of fire and consequently my sufferings.”
1159.explanation: Bhai Gurdas describes separation from the Beloved as a forest fire inside the body, which comforts only feed like oil. His Kabitt Savaiye are early exegesis, not scripture.
1159.tie_back: The Kural says ordinary fire burns only when touched, but love-sickness burns when one is far away; Bhai Gurdas likewise describes separation itself as a fire that blazes all the more in the Beloved's absence.
1159.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabitt Savaiye 668, English translation as given in the BaniDB database
1159._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (kabitt 668); good fit on separation as fire, but Bhai Gurdas lacks the Kural's pointed contrast between touching and moving away, and his Beloved is the Lord.

1160.quote_or_event: “Die before the one whom you love; to live after he dies is to live a worthless life in this world.”
1160.explanation: Guru Angad says that a true lover would rather die first than go on living once the beloved is gone.
1160.tie_back: The Kural's heroine says, with irony, that many seem able to bear separation and live on afterwards, implying she is not one of them; Guru Angad says outright that such a life after the beloved is worthless.
1160.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 83, Sri Raag ki Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1160._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa, two lines of one salok); strong fit on refusing to live on after losing the beloved, though Guru Angad speaks of a beloved who dies, not one who travels, and Sikh commentary reads it as self-surrender to the Lord.
